item.title: Bangladesh’s persistent real-wage crisis
item.description:
For nearly five years, ordinary working families across Bangladesh have been caught in a relentless economic vice.
According to recent Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) data, inflation has outpaced wage growth for 56 consecutive months, with September seeing wage growth dip to 7.9% (down from 8.05% in August) while living costs remain stubbornly high.
Inflation in Bangladesh rose to 8.34% in September 2026, as per BBS data, up slightly from 8.26% in August.
This structural imbalance forms the core of a deepening livelihood crisis—one where household incomes are structurally bypassed by compounding commodity prices.
This wage-inflation disconnect does not happen in a vacuum. It intersects directly with two other defining pressures highlighted in recent economic findings: the soaring rate of household debt and sluggish industrial recovery.
Recent BBS special surveys on living standards reveal that 47.42% of families are taking on debt just to run their households, with rural areas bearing the heaviest burden (51.91% of rural households borrowing to survive, compared to 40.19% in urban areas and 32.11% in city corporations).
Nationally, average monthly household expenses stand at Tk35,311 against an average income of just Tk33,513, creating an immediate monthly deficit.
When paired with the 56-month wage squeeze, the connection is stark: stagnant wages force families to bridge their monthly shortfalls either by depleting past savings or falling into informal, high-interest debt loops.
Economists point out that this is driven by deeper labor market vulnerabilities.
Hossain Zillur Rahman, executive chairperson of the Power and Participation Research Centre (PPRC), notes that the long gap between wages and inflation reflects broader economic stagnation and a shortage of productive employment rather than simple market forces.
Similarly, University of Dhaka economics professor Sayema Haque Bidisha highlights the absence of robust minimum-wage protection systems and regular wage adjustments in the informal sector.
Widespread informality, weak collective bargaining power, and an oversupplied labor market leave workers entirely vulnerable, with individual workers often seeing no pay increase even when changing jobs in labor-intensive sectors like poultry farms and brick kilns.
At the same time, policy and structural changes in trade and industry are attempting to navigate these headwinds.
Recent government moves to streamline industrial inputs—such as waiving prior approval requirements from the chief boiler inspector for boiler imports to ease manufacturing bottlenecks—aim to jump-start industrial productivity. Parallel initiatives, like the commercial revival of heritage textiles such as Dhakai Muslin (backed by multi-crore restoration projects), seek to spark specialized job creation and open global markets.
However, broader macroeconomic forecasts highlight that the road to recovery remains steep.
According to World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) outlooks for Bangladesh, persistent inflation, foreign exchange pressures, and slow investment growth continue to cloud the medium-term outlook.
The World Bank projects that ongoing economic pressures, weak job creation, and energy shortages could push the national poverty rate up to 22.5%, with extreme poverty rising past 10%.
Prices of daily commodities are unlikely to fall anytime soon. During the same period, average inflation could rise to 10.9%, predicted the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Research groups like PPRC similarly warn that vulnerable middle-income households are at high risk of slipping backward.
To break this 56-month cycle, economists emphasize that macroeconomic stabilization alone will not suffice.
Policymakers must pair inflation-taming monetary measures with robust labor market reforms, formalized wage protection in informal sectors, and targeted social safety net expansions to ensure that economic growth translates into tangible, purchasing-power gains for the working class.

item.title: Ishraque: Police unequipped, carried firearm for security during anti-drug operation
item.description:
Ishraque Hossain has defended carrying his personally licensed firearm during an anti-drug operation in Gandaria, saying the police were not adequately equipped to ensure security, while also announcing that he had sought voluntary release from his responsibilities as state minister for liberation war affairs.
The Dhaka-6 MP said he carried the firearm during the operation in Ghuntighar as a security measure.
Speaking at a press conference at the National Press Club on Monday, he said: “Since the police force is not equipped, I decided to eliminate drugs with the police and local residents. I informed the police station before going to Ghuntighar for the anti-drug operation. I carried my personally licensed firearm for my personal security.”
He also said: “The police force does not dare to go to Ghuntighar because they fire from above. Drugs were being introduced among school and college students in the Ghuntighar area of Gandaria. Based on complaints from local residents, I went to destroy the drug hub.”
Ishraque said drug traders had money and weapons, preventing local residents from speaking out. He described the Ghuntighar Munsirtek area as a notorious drug den and said the focus of the anti-drug operation had been diverted by creating various narratives.
“I have sought voluntary release from the post of state minister for liberation war affairs from the prime minister from today. He has granted me that opportunity,” he said.
Ishraque added: “The prime minister said, ‘You have started the war against drugs; continue it.’”
Explaining his decision, he said: “I expressed my intention to resign to the prime minister so that neither the prime minister’s activities nor the party would be embarrassed because of me.”
He also said: “If I have made any mistake or hurt anyone, I apologise. But I firmly believe that I have done nothing wrong. I carried a personal firearm for some time only for my own security.”
“I did not go to occupy land or collect extortion money. I went to eliminate drugs,” Ishraque said.
“There is collusion between drug control officials and an international syndicate,” he added.

item.title: Dinesh Trivedi joins Durga Puja celebrations in Dhaka
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi joined Durga Puja celebrations at several venues in Dhaka, extending greetings to devotees, students and organizers on the occasion of the Hindu festival.
Trivedi visited the Durga Puja festivities at Jagannath Hall of the University of Dhaka, where he shared the festive spirit with students, organizers and devotees.
On the occasion of Maha Ashtami, he inaugurated the distribution of Mahaprasad at Dhakeshwari National Temple, joining devotees in observing the religious festival.
He also visited Ramna Kali Mandir, where he conveyed his best wishes to devotees celebrating Durga Puja.
The Indian High Commissioner attended celebrations organized by the Gulshan-Banani Sarbajanin Puja Foundation in Dhaka and extended greetings to the organizers and devotees.
Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community, is celebrated across Bangladesh with religious rituals, cultural programs and gatherings at temples and makeshift pandals.

item.title: Govt cancels contracts of Sonali, Janata, Rupali bank MDs
item.description:
The government has cancelled the contractual appointments of the managing directors (MD) of three state-owned banks- Sonali Bank, Janata Bank, and Rupali Bank.
The decision was revealed in a letter, signed by Afroza Akter Riba, deputy secretary of the Financial Institutions Division under the Ministry of Finance, issued today.
The letter was sent to the chairmen of the three banks.
The ministry recommended cancelling the remaining terms of Sonali Bank MD Shawkat Ali Khan, Rupali Bank MD Kazi Md Wahidul Islam, and Janata Bank MD and CEO Mazibur Rahman.
Shawkat joined Sonali Bank as the MD on 30 October 2024 for a three-year term. Before that, he served as the MD of Bangladesh Krishi Bank.
Wahidul was appointed as the MD of Rupali Bank on 25 December 2024 for a three-year term. Mazibur was made MD and CEO of Janata Bank on 11 November 2024.
Following the cancellation of their remaining contractual terms, the boards of the respective banks will have to take further steps in accordance with the applicable rules.

item.title: Shama Obaed: MoFA aware of ex-air chief’s arrest, Home Ministry handling it
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Monday said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its mission in Qatar are aware of the arrest of former Air Force Chief Sheikh Abdul Hannan in Doha, adding that the Ministry stands ready to provide any assistance.
“It is entirely under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Ministry of Home Affairs is working on it,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in response to a question.
Hannan faces corruption and money laundering charges.
He was arrested in Doha, Qatar, on October 15, Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Secretary Saidur Rahman Khan told reporters on Sunday, adding that steps would be taken to bring him back to face the law in Bangladesh.
Air Chief Marshal (retd) Sheikh Abdul Hannan served as the 16th Chief of Air Staff of the Bangladesh Air Force from June 12, 2021, to June 11, 2024.
The ACC received informal information about his arrest on Saturday and officially confirmed it on Sunday through Interpol via the National Central Bureau (NCB) of Bangladesh Police.

item.title: Nasiruddin: Ishraque a victim of home minister's failure
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Chief Coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary on Monday said State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain has become a victim of the home minister's failure, referring to his resignation from the cabinet.
"The problem lies with the home minister. Ishraque has been caught up in this. The home minister commits the fault, but someone else has to pay for it," Nasiruddin said while talking to reporters after exchanging Durga Puja greetings at the Dhakeshwari National Temple in the capital.
He said Ishraque had entered politics with the intention of curbing drug-related activities, but got trapped due to the home minister's failures. “Ishraque's intentions were good, but he lost his ministerial post after falling into the trap.”
The NCP leader also raised concerns about the safety of the country’s Hindu community, saying despite the BNP government’s reported pledge to ensure security for all, members of the community are “not feeling well”.
"The BNP government has failed to provide them with proper security," he said, alleging that incidents of vandalism were reported in various places over the past three to four months.
Referring to the cow-slaughter incident at Jagannath University, Nasiruddin urged the Muslim community not to do anything that could anger, sadden or hurt Hindus.
He said no act should be committed that could hurt members of the Hindu community, suggesting sitting with them for discussions, if necessary.

item.title: Girls call for equal rights and action to end child marriage
item.description:
Child marriage, unequal access to education and health care, and concerns over safety remain key issues for adolescent girls in Bangladesh, who have called for stronger action to secure their rights and opportunities.
The call came at an event organized by Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) in Dhaka on Monday to mark International Day of the Girl Child 2026.
Held at Alok Auditorium in Mirpur-2 under the theme “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights,” the event brought together adolescent girls, civil society representatives and development partners to discuss child marriage, educational inequality, disability rights and the challenges girls face at home, in schools and online.
Addressing the event, Shaheen Anam, executive director of MJF, said celebrating girls’ achievements was insufficient without creating opportunities for them to exercise their rights.
“Simply saying that girls will conquer the world is not enough. We must ask how they will achieve that and what opportunities we are creating for them,” she said.
She said child marriage violated girls’ fundamental rights, including their ability to make decisions about their own lives, while undermining their education, health and future employment. Poverty, insecurity and a lack of alternatives often influenced families’ decisions to marry off their daughters, she added.
Shaheen Anam also questioned the effectiveness of existing child marriage prevention mechanisms, calling for stronger enforcement of laws and greater accountability from government institutions at the national and local levels.
Presenting the keynote, Lysa Mahmud Hema, assistant project manager at MJF, cited research findings showing that 47.2% of women aged 20–24 were married before turning 18, while 13.4% were married before the age of 15.
She also highlighted a decline in girls’ educational completion rates, from 91.3% at the primary level to 75.9% at the lower secondary level and 41.1% at the upper secondary level.
She called for greater investment in education, protection, health care, digital skills and girls’ participation in decisions affecting their lives.
During an intergenerational dialogue moderated by Nusrat Fatima, media and communication officer at MJF, adolescent girls shared their experiences of discrimination and challenged social norms restricting their choices.
Sumaiya Akter of SERAC Bangladesh stressed that education was essential for girls to make independent decisions.
Sadia Akter Eva, a student living in a shelter home associated with Maer Achol, highlighted unequal access to sports facilities, saying boys often received more time and resources.
Tasneem Ferdousi, a student of BISC, questioned the social perception that girls were ready for marriage after puberty, despite being children who lacked the emotional maturity to manage a household and raise children.
Other participants highlighted menstruation-related stigma, ethnic discrimination, language barriers and difficulties accessing education.
Ayesa Akter, an adolescent girl with a visual impairment, called for accessible learning materials, including Braille and audio resources, saying girls with disabilities needed equal rights and opportunities rather than sympathy.
Wadifa Rahman Apshara of SFX Greenherald International School also urged the government, communities and educational institutions to address the widening gap in educational completion.
Roksana Sultana, executive director of Breaking the Silence; Nishath Sultana, director of influencing campaign and communications at Plan International Bangladesh; and SM Shaikat, executive director of SERAC-Bangladesh, also spoke at the event.
Speakers said poverty, climate vulnerability and safety concerns continued to push families toward child marriage despite girls’ achievements in education and sports.
The program also featured cultural performances by children associated with Maer Achol.
In his closing remarks, Wasiur Rahman Tonmoy, lead of youth and social cohesion at MJF, thanked the participating girls, partner organizations and development partners, including the European Union, Global Affairs Canada, the Embassy of Switzerland, Plan International Bangladesh and Nagorikata CEF.
The event concluded with a call for concrete action to keep girls in education, protect them from violence and child marriage, and ensure their equal participation in society.

item.title: What is the metro rail schedule for Durga Puja holidays?
item.description:
Dhaka’s metro rail will operate on a special schedule during the Durga Puja holidays, with services following the regular timetable on October 20-22 and 24. On October 23, trains will run only from the afternoon.
Train intervals will range from 10 to 20 minutes depending on the time of day and passenger demand, according to Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (DMTCL).
The DMTCL operations department shared the schedule on Monday.
According to the schedule, the first train from Uttara North to Motijheel will depart at 6:30am, while the first train from Motijheel to Uttara North will leave at 7:15am on the four days.
For most of the day, trains will run at intervals of 10 to 12 minutes. At night, the intervals will increase to 15 to 20 minutes depending on passenger demand.
A total of 171 trips will operate in both directions on each of the four days.
On October 23, services from Uttara North to Motijheel will begin at 3pm, while trains from Motijheel to Uttara North will start at 3:20pm. A total of 82 trips will operate in both directions that day.
DMTCL said two additional trains would be kept ready at Platform 1 of Uttara North station and at the depot to manage passenger demand. The trains will be deployed as needed to adjust service intervals.

item.title: Siblings killed, parents injured in crash en route to Puja celebrations
item.description:
Two siblings were killed and four others injured when a cattle-laden locally made motorised vehicle (Nasimon) overturned onto a passenger van in Jhikargacha upazila of Jessore on Monday evening, police said.
The deceased were identified as Shovon, 10, and Disha, 3, the son and daughter of Sadhon Kumar, a resident of Mishrideara village in the upazila. Sadhon Kumar is a teacher at Jessore Cantonment College.
Golam Kibria Hasan, officer-in-charge (OC) of Jhikargacha Police Station, confirmed the incident.
Locals said Sadhon Kumar was travelling with his wife and two children to celebrate puja in their locality.
The accident occurred around 6:15pm on Council Road in the Phultala area of Magura Union when their van collided with a cattle-laden nasimon. The nasimon overturned onto the van, leaving Shovon and Disha dead on the spot.
Sadhon Kumar, his wife, the driver of the nasimon and one of its passengers were also injured in the accident.
The driver was taken to Jashore General Hospital for treatment.
The bodies of the two children were kept at Jhikargacha Upazila Health Complex.

item.title: House of Han opens at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport
item.description:
House of Han, a specialty Chinese restaurant led by Master Chinese Chef Chen, opened at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport on Sunday, introducing a dining concept centered on traditional Chinese cuisine, culinary craftsmanship and what its management describes as “honest luxury”.
The restaurant combines Chinese culinary traditions with contemporary presentation, elegant interiors and personalized hospitality, aiming to offer an authentic Chinese dining experience in the capital.
According to the restaurant, its menu reflects Chef Chen’s approach to Chinese cooking, drawing on traditional techniques, heritage and time-honored flavors while incorporating his own creative expression.
Duck is among the restaurant’s signature offerings, with its preparation, carving and presentation forming an integral part of the dining experience.
Speaking at the launch, Ashwani Nayar, area general manager for IHG Southwest Asia and cluster general manager for Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport and InterContinental Dhaka, said House of Han represents Chef Chen’s culinary vision.
“Our ambition is to bring honest, authentic Chinese cuisine to Dhaka in a setting that is equally luxurious. From the flavors on the plate to the interiors and the warmth of our service, every element has been thoughtfully considered,” he said.
Describing the restaurant’s concept in 2 words, Nayar said: “honest luxury”.
Chef Chen said Chinese cuisine is deeply rooted in heritage, respect for ingredients and techniques passed down through generations.
“At House of Han, my aim is to honor those traditions while bringing my own creativity and care to every dish. I look forward to welcoming guests to my table and sharing the flavors and craftsmanship that make this cuisine so special,” he said.
Located at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport, the restaurant is designed to accommodate business meetings, family gatherings and special celebrations.
It features 10 private dining rooms for guests seeking privacy and personalized service, providing spaces for business discussions and private occasions with family and friends.
With its opening, House of Han joins Dhaka’s growing fine-dining landscape, placing traditional Chinese culinary practices, contemporary presentation and hospitality at the center of its offering.

item.title: Six get life terms for gang-raping housewife in Tangail
item.description:
A Tangail court on Monday sentenced six men to life imprisonment with hard labour for gang-raping a housewife in Delduar upazila.
Judge A N M Ilias of the Tangail Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal delivered the verdict around noon. The convicts are: Rajon Mia, son of Hazrat Ali of Mangalhor village; Md Rifat, son of Majnu Mia; Abdur Rouf, son of Md Mobarak; Amir Hamza, son of Md Nilu Mia of Payla Paschimpara in Tangail Sadar; Al Amin, son of Nurul Islam of Pauli village in Kalihati; and Biplob Mia, son of late Siraj Mia of Pathrail village in Delduar.
The court also fined each of them Tk1 lakh, with an additional one year of imprisonment without hard labour if they fail to pay the fine.
Tangail public prosecutor Omrao Khan Dipu confirmed the matter.
According to the case statement, the victim went to her aunt’s house in Atia village of Delduar on October 29, 2024. She had borrowed Tk50,000 from her aunt due to a family dispute.
That night, while she was on her way to Madarjani, the accused allegedly forced her into an office room of Mohan Textile Mill and raped her in turns. They also took her mobile phone and Tk50,000 from her purse.
Police rescued her after receiving a call through the national emergency service 999.
The following day, she filed a case with Delduar Police Station. After investigation, Inspector (Unarmed) Azizul Haque Howlader submitted a charge sheet to the court.
Omrao Khan Dipu said the court delivered the verdict after a lengthy hearing and recording statements from witnesses, as the charges against the accused were proven.
The convicts were sent to Tangail District Jail after the verdict.

item.title: First accused in July uprising case freed after acquittal
item.description:
Former Ashulia police sub-inspector (SI) Sheikh Abzalul Haque, who turned state witness in a crimes against humanity case over the burning of six protesters’ bodies during the July uprising, has been released from prison following his acquittal.
He is the first accused in a July uprising case to be released after being acquitted by the International Crimes Tribunal.
Tribunal-2 acquitted him on February 5, and he was released from Kashimpur Central Jail-2 in Gazipur on October 13, the prison’s Jailer Md Arifur Rahman confirmed on Monday afternoon.
In the case, six accused, including former MP Saiful Islam, were sentenced to death, seven were handed life imprisonment, and two others were sentenced to seven years in prison. Abzalul Haque was acquitted.
A total of 16 people were accused in the case. Eight have been arrested, while the remaining eight are absconding.
The seven other arrested accused are former Savar Circle Additional Superintendent of Police Md Shahidul Islam, former Dhaka Additional Superintendent of Police Abdullahil Kafi, former Dhaka District Detective Branch (DB) Inspector Md Arafat Hossain, former Ashulia police sub-inspectors Abdul Malek, Arafat Uddin and Kamrul Hasan, and former police constable Mukul Chokdar.
Former MP Muhammad Saiful Islam is among the absconding accused.
The case was filed with the International Crimes Tribunal on September 11 over the killing of seven people in Ashulia on August 5, 2024, the day Sheikh Hasina was ousted from power. The charges included burning the bodies of six victims.

item.title: Government employees to retain existing allowance rates under new pay scale
item.description:
Government employees will continue receiving allowances at existing rates even after the introduction of a new national pay scale, according to a notification issued by the Finance Division on Monday.
The notification from the Ministry of Finance clarified that the existing allowance rates will remain in effect despite the introduction of the new pay structure.
The notification applies to employees of various government ministries, divisions, offices, agencies, state-owned enterprises and autonomous institutions.
Meanwhile, government officials and employees will begin receiving higher salaries this month, with the necessary budgetary allocation already made.
The government has stipulated that allowances will continue to be paid as a percentage of existing basic salaries until the basic salaries set under the 2026 Pay and Allowances Order come into effect.
The notification on the pay and allowances order was issued on September 19, exactly 1 month before the latest notification. The government had previously announced that allowances under the new pay structure would be implemented later.
Under the new pay structure, the minimum basic salary has been set at Tk20,000 and the maximum at Tk1,56,000. Although the structure took effect on July 1, the government decided to implement the full salary increases in phases over the 2026-27 and 2027-28 fiscal years.
The basic salary will be implemented in 3 phases: the first from July 1 to December 31 this year, the second from January 1 to June 30, 2027, and the third from July 1 to December 31, 2027.
Allowances under the new structure will take effect on January 1, 2028.
The process of determining government employees' salaries online under the new national pay structure is underway and is scheduled to be completed on Tuesday.
Since October 5, government employees have been entering the required information through the "Pay Fixation" option on the government's Integrated Budget and Accounting System (iBAS++) platform.
According to Finance Division sources, government employees will receive higher salaries at the end of this month. The necessary budgetary allocation has been made for this purpose.

item.title: Greek coast guard says 12 migrants die in Aegean sea crossings
item.description:
Twelve migrants died Monday attempting to cross the Aegean Sea, including six people on a boat that collided with a police vessel, authorities said.
A baby and four women were among six people who died off the island of Lesbos on Monday following the collision, a coast guard official told AFP.
The other six dead -- five men and a woman -- were on a small boat that capsized off the island of Samos, the coast guard added. Fourteen people on the boat, one of them a presumed Iranian organizer, were rescued.
The coast guard official said that in the incident off Lesbos, “a speedboat carrying migrants collided with the port side of a police patrol vessel.” The official said eight people were rescued.
There was no indication of the nationalities of either the victims or the people rescued.
The Aegean is a much-used route for migrants setting out from Turkiye hoping to reach Europe. There have been many deaths.
At least 15 migrants died in February off the Greek island of Chios when their boat collided with a coastguard patrol vessel.
One person died and 25 remain missing after a boat filled with migrants sank off the island of Gavdos, near Crete in September.
“Smugglers are putting migrants in grave danger,” Thanos Plevris, the migration minister who backs a very strict migration policy, told Ertnews public broadcaster, praising the coast guard.
“They are doing everything they can to save lives whilst at the same time protecting our borders,” he argued.
Greece is one of five European countries -– with Austria, Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands -– working to set up detention centers in Africa to which migrants whose asylum claims have been turned down can be sent.
This initiative does not however have unanimous EU support, with France notably opposed.
According to the EU Agency for Asylum, the 27 member states received 332,000 applications for international protection in the first half of this year, a 17% decrease on the same period in 2025 as countries tighten their migration policies.

item.title: AIUB hosts 4th International Conference on Computing Advancement
item.description:
The Department of Computer Science at American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) organized the 4th International Conference on Computing Advancement (ICCA 2026) on October 15–16, 2026.
The conference received more than 900 research paper submissions from 17 countries, with 214 selected for presentation. Research contributions came from Bangladesh and 17 other countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Japan and Canada.
Topics included artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, the Internet of Things (IoT), cybersecurity, data science and blockchain technology.
Ishtiaque Abedin, founder member and vice chairman of the AIUB Board of Trustees and secretary general of the Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB), attended the inaugural ceremony as chief guest.
Other attendees included Dr Carmen Z Lamagna, former AIUB vice chancellor and Board of Trustees member; Professor Dr Saiful Islam, AIUB vice chancellor; Professor Dr Dip Nandi, dean of the Faculty of Science and Technology (FST) and conference program chair; Professor Dr Khandaker Tabin Hasan, FST associate dean and conference general chair; and Professor Dr Md Abdur Razzaque, chairperson of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Dhaka.
Dr Hasanul A Hasan, founder member and chairman of the AIUB Board of Trustees, attended the closing ceremony on October 16 as chief guest. Other attendees included Ms Nadia Anwar, founder member of the AIUB Board of Trustees; Professor Dr Md Abdur Rahman, pro vice chancellor; Professor Dr Manzur H Khan, proctor; and other senior university officials.
Certificates and commemorative mementos were presented to organizers and participants at the closing ceremony.
AIUB said the conference aimed to promote research, innovation and international collaboration in computing and technology.

item.title: Giving old watches a second life
item.description:
Partho Pretom Sarker wears a Citizen. It has, what I’m told, a “tiger-eye” dial,and was made in Japan sometime in the 1980s.
He didn't buy it new, and that was the whole point.
At just 19 years old, he goes looking for old mechanical watches that he then brings back to life.
“People say men are not sentimental,” he says. “I think that is wrong. A man will walk five kilometres for a ten-taka cup of tea from one specific stall not because the tea is better, but the memory or the importance the tea stall holds.”
Photo: Courtesy
Watches, in his telling, work the same way. Nobody's nostalgic about the object. They're nostalgic about the hands that potentially used to wear it. They are nostalgic about the time period.
So why does he do it? To understand, you have to go back further than Partho does. Much further.
Right after 1971, Bangladeshi men started leaving for the Middle East in serious numbers, chasing work in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, and Malaysia.
They came home eventually, and they came home with gifts. The most popular thing to bring back for your loved ones, your father, brother or even for yourself, was a mechanical watch.
A Seiko or a Citizen wasn't just a watch. It was proof you'd been somewhere. It read as competence, as status.
Then quartz happened, and none of that mattered anymore.
From the mid-'70s onward, battery-powered watches flooded the market. No more winding, no maintenance. The big Japanese watchmakers -- Seiko, Citizen, Orient -- pivoted hard into mass production.
Some Swiss brands retreated into pure luxury. Smaller names just disappeared.
And in Dhaka, a small community of watchmakers who'd trained abroad and had come home to service the mechanical watches watched their skills go quiet.
By the time the century turned, Dhaka's mechanical watches had ended up in one of two places -- the back of a drawer or the bin.
This is where Partho comes in, sourcing old watches from collectors.
Not everything he finds can be saved. Knowing which watch is worth restoring and which one is beyond it is, he says, half the actual craft.
What survives goes to the handful of technicians left in the country who still remember how to disassemble a mechanical movement, clean it, regulate it, and put it back together without losing a spring. Then it finds someone new to belong to.
A lot of what comes through the door isn't for sale at all. Like a grandfather's watch that stopped ticking sometime in the '90s and never got looked at again. “The watch was never really gone,” Partho says. “It just needed someone who knew how to bring it back.”
He owns a business named “Bengal Curator.” Naming the business “Curator” wasn't an accident, either.
He talks about it as an act of resistance against a very specific, very current condition-- a mass-produced world.
Finding something old and beautiful, and actually giving it attention, started to feel like a strange, almost radical thing to do.
If that sounds like a Gen Z problem dressed up in old brass and steel, that's because it is.
Fast fashion has a sibling nobody talks about as much: Fast everything. Fast phones, fast furniture, fast relationships to objects that used to be built to outlive their owners.
Partho didn't start Bengal Curator as some tidy act of cultural preservation, and he doesn't pretend otherwise.
“I built this business out of survival,” he says. It became about love for the objects later.
Maybe that’s the difference between a heritage project funded by someone else's money, and a university student actually needing this to work.
When asked about the work life balance, he said he follows the 80-20 rule.
Eighty percent of what actually moves the needle comes from twenty percent of the work you put in, so the real skill isn't grinding harder, it's figuring out which twenty percent is worth grinding on at all.
That's how he's kept a business, a university degree, and something resembling a social life all running at once without any of them collapsing.
The harder part, he says, wasn't the watches. It was learning to talk to people who'd already decided, on sight, that he was too young to be trusted.
Business in Dhaka, he's found, doesn't run on spreadsheets nearly as much as people assume. It runs on relationships, on trust built slowly.
And the older generation wants to see you've earned the right to be taken seriously before they'll hand you anything real.
What he's actually chasing, underneath the watches themselves, is memories.
Memories of people saving up for a watch, to wear it to a wedding, to gift their loved ones.
Partho wants to hand that memory down, instead of throwing it out. The exact opposite of what the world is like today.
Partho's watch still keeps decent time, all these decades later. Somebody, back in the 1980s, thought carefully enough about buying it that it survived long enough to end up on his wrist.

item.title: Why visual art remains distant from the public eye
item.description:
Think about the last time a song really got to you, maybe a Baul song you heard late at night that left a heavy feeling in your chest you couldn’t quite explain, or a Nazrul Geeti whose beat lifted you right up, and I am sure most of us can also remember getting lost inside a Tagore poem or a novel we didn’t want to finish.
Now think about the last time you stood in front of a painting, say one of Zainul Abedin’s famine sketches with those thin, starving bodies or one of S M Sultan’s strong and dream-like farmers, and ask yourself honestly what you felt.
For a lot of us, I think the answer is not much, just a kind of distance.
I believe this gap comes from the way we are brought up, as from our first day in school we are taught to read words and make sense of them, and in all those years hardly anyone sits us down to show us that a picture can be read too.
Literature works through language, so people can walk into the world of a story or a poem using words they already know, though to be fair a lot of it still goes over the head of the common reader. But literature at least has a place in our classrooms; it is part of the syllabus and it has had some support and care from society, more or less.
Painting is different as it works through the eye and does not hand us a clear meaning in plain words, so for ordinary people in our country it is not an easy thing to get into, and the support it gets from our society is very small too.
We grew up hearing about Zainul Abedin and how great he was, his best-known works keep showing up in our exam questions and his images are even printed on our money, which tells you how famous he is.
Yet has anyone ever actually stopped to tell us what makes those paintings so powerful, what it is exactly that makes them good?
And what about Sultan, his farmers with their huge god-like bodies, the round gatherings of farmers and cattle, all those hard-working people painted so big and grand, living together with their land and their animals almost like one family.
Why do their faces look so divine? What are they trying to tell us, and what is the painting making us feel? I honestly wonder whether anyone is even talking about this.
When Sultan’s birth anniversary comes around, our job seems to end with an article about his life in the newspaper (and I am aware this is a newspaper page too), and knowing about an artist’s life does matter, but when it comes to sitting with the paintings themselves and looking closely at what they do we go almost completely quiet.
Part of the problem I think is that we want a painting to give us its message straight away like a headline does, and its power actually works in a much quieter and deeper way that takes time.
A painting is more than a decoration for the wall or a hobby for rich people, I like to think of it as a piece of glass that light passes through and comes out the other side in many colours, so when we look at it properly it opens up many meanings, feelings and ideas, and in its own silent way it plays a big part in shaping who we are as a society.
So, if we want to understand what a painting is saying, maybe we should start with a simple question.
We can ask of any kind of art, a song, a poem, a novel or a painting, which is what does it make us feel, and what kind of experience does it give us that wakes up our sense of beauty and our emotions?
Take a song, the feeling it wakes up in us is tied to the seven basic notes, the way they sit with one another to make a tune, and the beat, then the words come pouring out on top of that same tune. In a poem it is mostly about how the language is used along with the rhythm, to tell us about something that happened or some idea about life.
A novel has room to describe events in detail, so we live through the exciting moments of a character’s life, we see where their choices lead them and we come away a bit wiser from the story.
If you look at all of these together you will notice that each one is a piece of real life mixed in with the artist’s own way of thinking.
A painting works the same way. The artist picks out small broken pieces from real events and puts them together into one whole and this full experience, made of what happened and what the artist thought about it. Slowly arrives at some kind of end point which becomes the artist’s purpose, the reason the painting exists in the first place.
Then the artist fills it with colour, line and space to make a picture, a world where everything the artist saw and felt can live, and if we as viewers manage to step inside that world we can walk around in it with our own understanding, and the longer we stay and think, the more of a story it starts telling us.
It is this purpose of the artist that makes real life look so different from one painting to the next, and this is also what separates a painting from a photograph.
A photograph gives us a copy of an ordinary scene, but if several artists painted that same scene, each of them would show it in their own way as each one is painting it for a different reason.
Making art also has a real, physical side to it beyond imagination and deep thinking, which is skill in particular methods, the craft, and the finish that give a painting its own colour and shape.
A good painting needs two things that the artist has worked on for years: the ability to see beneath the outside look of things, and the beauty of the craft itself, and the artist gives the picture its shape by keeping these two in balance; as if one of them is missing, then the real thought behind the painting never fully comes through.
What I want to do with this writing is to understand why this distance between us and paintings exists, who is to blame for it and gain some basic insight into painting itself: how it's done and how it's delivering meaning.
I think we need to see how our education system, with all its gaps, and the fact that art so rarely reaches ordinary people, have together pushed painting away from the common person.
We also need to understand that a painting can wake a society up just as strongly as a song or a poem can and get people thinking for themselves. And lastly, we need someone to walk us through the basics of a painting, how it is put together, and how an artist thinks so that we can enter that world properly and slowly build our own way of judging what we see.
So, the next time you come across a painting, in a gallery, or even on a page of an old-school textbook, I would ask you to stay with it a little longer than usual and ask it what it is trying to make you feel. You might be surprised by how much it has been waiting to say.
Sharif Al Zubayer Zishan is an aspiring writer and journalist.

item.title: Cantonment board services added to MyGov platform
item.description:
Citizen services provided by all cantonment boards have been brought under the MyGov platform through an initiative of the Directorate of Military Lands and Cantonments to establish a technology-driven, transparent and citizen-friendly service system.
The initiative was implemented under the overall supervision of the Cabinet Division, with support from the Aspire to Innovate (a2i) Program and the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Division.
Under the previous system, service recipients had to visit cantonment board offices in person to obtain services. Applications, document submissions, fee payments and certificate collection were handled manually, often requiring multiple visits and resulting in additional expenses, time and inconvenience.
To reduce travel, time, expenses and inconvenience for citizens, a pilot project was initially launched by incorporating 2 citizen services of the Dhaka Cantonment Board into the MyGov platform. Following the successful pilot, steps were taken to digitize services at the remaining 14 cantonment boards.
As part of the process, 3 service analysis workshops were held in March 2026, with officials and employees from the 14 cantonment boards participating. A total of 63 types of citizen services were reviewed and analyzed, and 19 basic services were identified for digitization. Subsequently, 185 online application forms were developed for these services across different cantonment boards.
In June and July 2026, 7 region-based validation workshops were held to verify and finalize the online application forms, service fees, service workflows and templates.
In August and September, 140 officials and employees, including Cantonment Executive Officers from all cantonment boards, received practical training. This completed the necessary preparations for managing services and conducting operations through the digital platform.
Currently, 185 online application forms covering 19 basic services are publicly available on the MyGov platform. Citizens can apply online from home, pay applicable service fees and receive certificates or services containing QR codes.
They can also monitor the progress of their applications online and provide feedback on the services.
Cantonment boards can receive, verify, investigate, process and dispose of applications online through the same platform. This is expected to accelerate administrative activities, reduce paperwork and strengthen transparency and accountability in service management.
As part of the current government's priorities for simplifying services and digital transformation, the inclusion of cantonment board citizen services on the MyGov platform has opened a new avenue for integrated, technology-driven service management.

item.title: Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power
item.description:
The concerns raised by rights organizations and media advocates over the proposed changes to the Cyber Protection Act, 2026, deserve serious consideration. We agree that the government must recognize that any legislation intended to protect cyberspace must not become a tool for silencing dissent.
The proposed provisions concerning defamation, maligning, rumours, and misinformation are particularly worrying because vague definitions can easily be misused. When the law leaves too much room for interpretation, legitimate criticism, investigative journalism, and public-interest reporting may become grounds for legal harassment.
The possibility of arbitrary content restrictions and punitive action against media outlets makes these concerns even more pressing.
Bangladesh has already witnessed how cyber laws can be weaponized against journalists, critics, and ordinary citizens. We cannot allow a new legal framework to reproduce the same failures under a different name.
Changing governments must also mean changing the practices that undermine democratic rights. Otherwise, promises of reform amount to little more than rhetoric.
There is, of course, a need to address genuine cybercrime, online harassment, and other harmful activities, but these objectives must be pursued through clearly defined offences, due process, independent oversight, and meaningful safeguards for freedom of expression.
The government must consult journalists, legal experts, civil society organizations, and digital rights advocates before advancing legislation that affects the fundamental rights of millions.
More importantly, any and all further attempts to stifle our freedom of speech must be dealt with promptly and decisively. This requires more than assurances that a law will not be misused -- it requires enforceable protections, transparent procedures, and accountability whenever authorities overstep their powers.
Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted by those in power. It is a fundamental right that allows citizens to question authority and hold institutions accountable.
It's time the government shows us that it understands this distinction. We cannot keep repeating the same mistakes at the cost of our freedom of speech.

item.title: The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon
item.description:
State Minister Ishraque Hossain’s decision to resign -- following public outrage over footage of him brandishing a firearm during an anti-drug operation -- is an important development. However, his resignation must not be allowed to end the dialogue about his conduct or the responsibilities of elected representatives.
Let us be clear: Ishraque's actions were not part of a minister’s role, and under no circumstances can they be misconstrued as valid or acceptable.
Ministers are entrusted with political leadership and the responsibility of ensuring that state institutions function effectively. An elected government must strengthen relevant agencies, provide them with adequate resources, ensure that they can perform their duties without political interference, as well as hold them accountable if they fail to do so.
It must be understood: We have not elected MPs to take the law into their own hands, nor should the public be encouraged to view such conduct as a heroic demonstration of strength.
Allowing elected officials to assume law enforcement roles risks undermining established procedures, weakening institutional authority, and setting a dangerous precedent. The rule of law cannot depend on who holds a weapon or occupies a position of power.
Drug trafficking is most certainly a serious problem that demands sustained action. However, an effective anti-drug campaign must be conducted through lawful procedures, professional investigations, and accountable enforcement.
No individual, regardless of political position or stated intentions, should be exempt from these standards.
Ishraque’s resignation must also not be taken as a substitute for accountability. The circumstances surrounding the incident must be examined, and any violation must be addressed through due process.
Such conduct cannot be praised as decisive leadership or ignored because its stated objective is an important one.
Strong institutions, not individual displays of power, are what protect the public and build trust in the state. The government must demonstrate that elected representatives are expected to uphold the law, not bypass it.

item.title: In art, a wall of heritage and an artificial message of division
item.description:
Even before Bangladesh was born as an independent state, the country’s cultural arena has been a battleground. This fight is not waged with shields and swords. It has mainly been carried on through the narrative of “religion versus culture.” Should the ancient culture of the Bengali people, which bears the strong influence of Sanatani (Hindu), Buddhist and Islamic faiths, be the foundation of national and state identity in this land? Or should the character of this state rest only on the religious identity of its Muslim-majority citizens, where language and culture from the Arab-Persian region count for more than Bengal’s own culture?
There is no reason to doubt the narrow communal mindset hidden inside this debate and this division, and these days it is hardly hidden at all. It is also undeniable that this debate plays an important role in Bangladesh’s political divisions. Above all, it was through this very division that attempts were made in 1970 and 1971 to block the emergence of Bangladesh as an independent country. But the 1970 election and the Liberation War of 1971 defeated that effort, and Bangladesh was born on the basis of Bengali cultural identity.
Recent events show that the stirring-up of the country’s origin, identity and basis of existence through that narrow debate, which began after the 2024 change of power, has not yet died down. The anti-Liberation War mindset that raised its head under the interim Yunus government is now being revived. Those who destroyed the Sheikh Mujib Memorial Museum at Road 32 in Dhanmondi to erase the history of the Liberation War, and who vandalized sculptures related to Bangabandhu and the Liberation War across the country, are now trying to strike at the very foundation of independence by a new route.
Distortion of history
Recently, the walls along a road in Dhaka were decorated with portraits of some leading figures of Bengali culture. Many welcomed this initiative by the city authorities on the wall beside the Shilpakala Academy. But then a campaign began on social media whose language, underlying message and purpose have become very familiar since the 2024 uprising. However crude the campaign’s methods, its aim is clear: T o crack the country’s cultural identity, to create division on the basis of religion, and to move the country’s birth from 1971 back to 1947, presenting Bangladesh as a product of the “two-nation theory.”
Freedom of dissent is important in every democratic society, even when that dissent amounts to distorting history. But it would be wrong to call what has been going on in Bangladesh for the past two years merely free expression. Alongside the rewriting of the nation’s history, there has been destructive activity, extreme intolerance of and threats against the pro-Liberation War narrative, and even communally provocative statements.
Some people on social media have asked why portraits of Satyajit Ray or Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar were placed beside those of Bangladesh’s eminent artist Zainul Abedin, the actor Humayun Faridi or the national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam. Their argument is that Ray and Vidyasagar are not “Bangladeshi.” Those who say this surely understand very well that “Bangladeshi” identity is not the point here. These figures were chosen for their mountainous contributions to Bengali culture. That is exactly their problem. But there, communalism is visibly playing a big part.
Nazrul and the nation
For example, there is no fuss about the portrait of Kazi Nazrul Islam, Bangladesh’s national poet. There is no reason for any. Just as there should be no controversy over Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, there should be no objection to Nazrul either, because both are Bengali and both made extraordinary contributions to Bengali literature and culture. Like Vidyasagar, Kazi Nazrul Islam was also an Indian. So why object to one of them? Because he is Hindu?
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman brought Nazrul to Bangladesh in 1972 and allotted a house in Dhanmondi for his whole family. Nazrul was not only a leading figure in Bengali-language literature; in the backdrop of the Liberation War, he was a source of inspiration for the people. Nazrul’s poems and songs gave the people courage and inspiration in 1971. After independence, the government of independent Bangladesh felt fulfilled at being able to bring him close, and the people were happy and proud to see him with their own eyes.
The tragedy was that Nazrul had lost his understanding and his speech many years before coming to Dhaka. How much he understood that he had come to Dhaka as a guest of a newly independent state is open to question. But it was probably because of the state honour he received in Dhaka that Nazrul’s family stayed on in Bangladesh.
Nazrul was born in India, spent his whole life in India, and was an Indian. He did not become a Bangladeshi overnight by spending the last four years of his life in Dhaka. Yet there is no controversy or question anywhere about declaring Nazrul the national poet of Bangladesh. There should not be. Likewise, there should be no question or controversy about adopting a song written by Rabindranath Tagore as the national anthem. But here too, out of exactly the same communal mindset, controversy has been created over Rabindranath, a follower of the Brahmo Samaj, and over his song “Amar Shonar Bangla.”
The drama and the police response
A drama of erasing Rabindranath’s portrait from the wall of the Shilpakala Academy was also staged recently. It has to be called a drama because, while a woman was about to deface Rabindranath’s portrait with ink, countless people were seen around her filming on their phones, and perhaps one or two were even live-streaming. At that very moment, a policeman ran up and stopped her!
The whole incident looked like a publicity stunt. But afterwards the police filed a “sedition” case against the woman and four people from her organization , arranging even more publicity for them. The communal mindset of an organization that exists in name only, expressed through vandalism, may be seen as a nuisance. But whether it is reasonable to treat it as outright “sedition” is a question that can certainly be asked.
Yet there is also a silver lining behind the dark cloud. On one hand, the police reaction seems excessive, especially when the alleged “crime” is essentially confined to a political statement. On the other hand, the authorities’ firmness deserves praise. Had the same incident happened under the Yunus government, the portraits of Satyajit Ray and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar might have been wiped off the Shilpakala Academy wall overnight. Perhaps the officials in charge at the city authority would have had to answer for it, and perhaps a job or two would have been at stake.
It goes without saying that the course of events will not stop here. The process of cutting the people of Bangladesh off from their cultural history and heritage, which began two years ago, will undoubtedly continue. Whether the government will confront this tendency, or stay indifferent like the Yunus government and in effect keep encouraging it, is a decision the BNP must make.
Instead of isolated reactions to isolated incidents and overreactions like the “sedition” case, it is time for the government to send a clear message. The foundation of Bangladesh’s birth is the language and culture of Bengalis irrespective of religion or caste. In the Bengali language, literature and the whole cultural arena, no division on the basis of religion, or of which side of the border someone was born on, is acceptable. The government must give this message clearly. Otherwise the possibility will remain that this artificial division turns into political, social and communal conflict.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Devotees flock to Kumari Puja in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
Devotees thronged a Durga Puja mandap at Gurucharan Roy’s Akhra in Brahmanbaria town on Monday as Kumari Puja was observed on Maha Ashtami, the eighth day of the Hindu festival.
Organised by the Town Sarbojanin Durga Puja Committee, the ritual involved worshipping Goddess Durga in the form of a young girl through traditional religious rites.
This year, 10-year-old Ishita Chakraborty was worshipped as the Kumari, drawing large crowds of devotees to the mandap from the afternoon.
Devotees Gayatri Saha, Rakesh Roy and Sanjay Saha said Kumari represents a manifestation of Goddess Durga. They noted that Swami Vivekananda introduced the practice of worshipping a young girl as the divine mother at Belur Math in 1901, after which the tradition gained popularity among devotees.
“We pray to the goddess in her Kumari form for the well-being of our families and everyone else. We also seek her blessings to destroy evil forces and establish peace through the triumph of good over evil,” they said.
Purohit Prosenjit Chakraborty of the Town Sarbojanin Durga Puja Mandap said, according to Hindu mythology, Kumari Puja is associated with the slaying of the demon Kolasura by the goddess in her maiden form.
According to the legend, Kolasura seized control of heaven and earth, prompting the distressed gods to seek the help of Goddess Mahakali. Responding to their prayers, the goddess took the form of a young girl and defeated the demon. The ritual of Kumari Puja is believed to have originated from this legend.
Earlier in the morning, devotees observed Sandhi Puja, a significant ritual marking the transition between Ashtami and Navami. The ceremony concluded with the lighting of 108 lamps.
In the evening, puja mandaps across the town were set to host dhunuchi dances and traditional arati rituals. Families were also expected to visit temples in groups to offer prayers and join the festivities.

item.title: Mosque, temple in same compound stand as symbols of communal harmony
item.description:
A mosque and a Hindu temple have stood side by side in the same courtyard in Tangail’s Nagarpur upazila for 56 years, with Muslims and Hindus maintaining a longstanding tradition of religious harmony and mutual respect.
At Chowdhury Bari, the Central Jame Mosque stands beside the Durga temple, where Durga Puja is celebrated every year. During the festival, the temple authorities stop the beating of drums and other loud music when the mosque’s call to prayer begins. The puja activities resume shortly after the prayers end.
The practice has continued for decades without any reported disputes over religious activities, offering an example of peaceful coexistence between the two communities.
The temple was established in 1932 as the Usha Thakur Central Durga Temple. The Chowdhury Bari Club was formed at the premises in 1969, after which Durga Puja began to be celebrated there regularly. The Central Jame Mosque was built in the same courtyard in 1972. Since then, Muslims have offered prayers at the mosque while Hindus have continued their religious rituals at the neighbouring temple.
During Durga Puja, the temple authorities suspend loud music during the call to prayer and congregational prayers at the mosque. Once the prayers end, the drums and other musical instruments resume, allowing both communities to observe their religious practices without disrupting one another.
Hindu worshippers said they had never faced any problems because of the mosque’s proximity to the temple. They credited the longstanding relationship to mutual respect and cooperation between the two communities.
“We have no problems with the mosque beside our temple. Muslims provide us with all possible support, and we also stop our puja activities during the call to prayer and namaz. This harmony has continued for generations. We live together like brothers, and we hope it will continue in the future,” a worshipper said.
Muslim residents also said there had been no disputes between the two communities. They said the temple authorities were aware of the mosque’s prayer schedule and adjusted their activities accordingly to avoid disturbing worshippers.
Abul Kalam, a Muslim resident, said the mosque and temple had shared the same courtyard for decades without any problems. He added that the temple authorities stopped their activities during prayers.
Amrita Saha, who has been visiting the temple during Durga Puja for several years, said Muslim residents regularly helped Hindu worshippers and ensured the celebrations proceeded without disruption.
The mosque’s imam said the Eidgah ground was also located near the mosque and temple, drawing large crowds during religious occasions. He said the temple authorities suspended puja activities during namaz and that Muslims extended their cooperation to the celebrations.
Liton Poddar, president of the Chowdhury Bari Club, said the two communities had never experienced any problems over their religious activities. He said the club followed the mosque committee’s prayer schedule, while the mosque committee also extended its support to the Puja celebrations.
Nagarpur Upazila Nirbahi Officer Likhon Banik said the arrangement at Chowdhury Bari reflected Bangladesh’s tradition of communal harmony, with Muslims and Hindus observing their religious practices in the same premises.
He said this year’s Durga Puja, like previous years, was being celebrated peacefully with the cooperation of both communities.
Local lawmaker Robiul Awal Lablu said Hindus and Muslims had long lived and worked together in the area without religious divisions. He added that they cooperated not only during religious festivals but also on various other issues, expressing hope that the longstanding bond would remain strong.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to visit Durga Puja mandaps in Rangpur, Rajshahi and Chittagong on Tuesday, marking what officials say the first visit by a head of government to Hindu community celebrations outside Dhaka during the Sharadiya festival.
PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon on Monday said the prime minister will visit Rangpur first in the morning, followed by Rajshahi and Chittagong.

Tarique Rahman will return to Dhaka on Tuesday night after visiting the puja mandaps in Chittagong, he added.
The prime minister is scheduled to leave Tejgaon Airport at 9:00 am by military aircraft for the three-district tour.
Earlier on Sunday night, he visited Durga Puja mandaps in Dhaka’s Mohakhali and Banani areas. His wife, Dr Zubaida Rahman, accompanied him during the visits.
Maha Nabami will be celebrated on Tuesday, while the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community will end on October 21 with the immersion of idols on Bijoya Dashami.
